Decision on Applicant's A1 submission and continued action
Summary
- The prior 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA second paragraph) rejection of claims 1-11 is withdrawn in view of Applicant's amendment to independent claim 1 and the specification support. The amendment to define the "complex structure" as a "mountain range-shaped microstructure and nano-fiber structures having a wire shape or a rod shape" resolves the prior indefiniteness concern. - The prior rejections under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102/103 remain outstanding for the reasons below. The Examiner sets forth the grounds and the reasoning and identifies the evidence of record. Applicant is invited to reply with arguments, evidence, or an interview request. Continued 35 U.S.C. 102/103 grounds (summary and reasoning)
1) Claims 1-3 and 6-8 (anticipation/obviousness over Wang; in the alternative obviousness in view of Raghuraman): The Office's November 30, 2016 action explained that Wang (as characterized in that action) teaches anodizing aluminum to produce an anodized (aluminum oxide) film having micro- and nano-scale features and further teaches formation of a hydrophobic monomolecular layer (trichlorooctadecyl-silane) on that anodized surface. The Office also noted that substitution of hydrophobic silane species (e.g., Applicant's recited HDFS) is an obvious or predictable variation supported by Raghuraman (or equivalent disclosures), and that a person of ordinary skill would understand that a silane monolayer will conform to the underlying surface topography. The record citation in the prior action is: "Claim(s) 1-3 and 6-8 is/are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) ... as anticipated by Wang" (IW40PYD7RXEAPX2). Applicant argues that Wang does not disclose the specific mountain-range/nano-fiber morphology recited in amended claim 1 and that the claimed surface provides different droplet removal behavior. The Examiner acknowledges Applicant's arguments and the amendment, but finds that the record (as relied upon in the Office action) still supports a prima facie showing that the combination of anodizing and monolayer surface modification in the prior art renders the claimed structural and functional result within the scope of the applied prior art. If Applicant disputes the factual premise (for example, that Wang lacks the claimed morphology), Applicant must either (a) point to specific passages/figures in the applied references that contradict the Office's characterization, or (b) supply objective evidence (declaration, comparative SEM data, or other experimental data) showing the prior art lack or showing an unexpected property achieved only by the claimed morphology that would rebut the Examiner's position. Absent such evidence, the rejection will be maintained. 2) Claims 4-5 (obviousness over Wang in view of Lerner): The prior action explained that Wang discloses anodizing and that Lerner discloses anodizing voltage as a result-effective variable and provides examples of higher voltages (up to 100 V) depending on material and film thickness; the Office relied upon this teaching to support selection of the claimed anodizing voltage/time/temperature ranges as within the ordinary skill of the art. See: "Claim 4 and 5 is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) ... as obvious over Wang ... and further in view of Lerner" (IW40PYD7RXEAPX2). Applicant's reply traversed this rejection but provided no comparative data or evidence of criticality or unexpected results across the claimed ranges. The Examiner finds the combination to present a prima facie case of obviousness because the cited references would have suggested selecting workable anodizing parameters (temperature, voltage, time) within the recited ranges by routine optimization. If Applicant believes the recited ranges are critical (i.e., produce unexpected results), submit comparative data or a declaration explaining the unexpected result over the closest prior art. 3) Claims 9-11 (obviousness over Wang in view of Gentleman and Shah): The prior action explained that Gentleman teaches condensers and tubes with hydrophobic coatings and that Wang teaches an anodized hydrophobic aluminum surface; combining these teachings to form coolant tubes or evaporator tubes with an anodized hydrophobic surface was found to be an obvious design choice. Shah was cited for teaching extended-surface fins and zigzag/ waveform fins. See: "Claim 9 is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) ... as obvious over Wang ... and further in view of Gentleman" and "Claims 10 and 11 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) ... as obvious over Wang ... and further in view of Gentleman and Shah" (IW40PYD7RXEAPX2). Applicant argues foreign allowances and that the combination fails to teach the claimed evaporator having the specific fabricated super-hydrophobic surface, but offers no comparative evidence demonstrating non-obviousness or a patentable distinction. The Examiner therefore maintains the 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections. Applicant options and response requirements

If an interview is desired, provide at least three proposed dates and times and the best telephone number. - If Applicant believes allowance is proper without further amendment, submit a detailed explanation specifically addressing the cited references and why each applied reference fails to teach or suggest each asserted limitation. - Examiner relied on the November 30, 2016 Office action for the factual characterizations of the cited prior art and the combinations made therein (document IW40PYD7RXEAPX2). That Office action is part of the record and is the basis for the outstanding rejections. - Applicant's amendments that overcame the 35 U.S.C. 112 issue are accepted into the record. Procedural and administrative
This is a non-final action on the merits (continued rejection). Respond within the statutory period or the application will be subject to final disposition in accord with practice. The Examiner is available for a conference if Applicant believes it would aid in resolving the outstanding issues.

applicant_argument_responses.response: The Examiner acknowledges the Applicant's arguments and the submission of field data and a declaration. However, the record shows Hutchins discloses gel-forming compositions that include silicates and polymeric gel-formers together with delayed-acting esters/anhydrides and gas precursors and discloses placing such compositions in subterranean formation pores to reduce permeability. The mere presence in Hutchins of colloidal/silicate and polymeric gel-formers (with delayed reaction chemistries) reads on the broad, generic claim limitations. Hutchins' teaching that ‘‘gel-forming ingredient’’ may be colloids and that delayed acting substances (e.g., esters, anhydrides) transform species in-situ supports the Examiner's position that Hutchins anticipates or renders obvious the claimed subject matter in absence of a clear limiting distinction in claim language. With respect to the asserted distinction (crosslinked vs non-crosslinked), the Hutchins disclosure includes a broad genus of gel-formers and does not limit the gel to only permanently crosslinked polymer networks; moreover, claim 1 and claim 11 as presently drafted do not require a particular, structural mechanism of gelation that would exclude Hutchins' teaching. Regarding the field data, the Examiner finds the submitted data and declaration do not, on their face, establish a commensurate, unexpected technical effect across the full scope of the claims. The declaration lacks the detailed, controlled comparative tests required to persuasively rebut a prima facie case of anticipation/obviousness: testing must compare treatments under the same operating conditions, using the same formation and treatment volumes, materials and procedures, and must show that the asserted improvement is attributable to the claimed structural limitation (here, the use of non-crosslinked polymers) rather than to other differences in operational parameters or compositions. Absent such persuasive, comparative evidence, the prior-art rejections are maintained. Applicant may rebut by (a) amending claims to recite structural or process limitations that distinguish over Hutchins (for example, explicit non-crosslinked polymer limitations tied to measurable properties or exclusion of gas- generating precursors), and/or (b) submitting detailed comparative data and an accompanying sworn declaration that demonstrates a statistically significant, unexpected advantage attributable to the claimed limitation and commensurate in scope with the claims.

Action on Application (Continuation-in-Part) — substantive reply to Applicant's A1 amendment and remarks
A. Summary
This action continues and maintains the Office’s prior rejections. The application remains under pre-AIA first-to-invent provisions. Applicant elected Group I claims (claims 1–7 and 11–19) for examination. The Examiner has considered Applicant’s September 9, 2016 amendments and arguments (including the submitted declaration and field data). The rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112(d) (improper dependent form), pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) (anticipation), and pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) (obviousness) are maintained for the reasons set forth below. The prior Office action (June 10, 2016) was made final; Applicant’s response did not overcome the deficiencies identified. This action is a continuation of that final action and continues the position that claims are unallowable in their present form.
B. Claim-form (35 U.S.C. 112) — Claim 19
1. Grounds and reasoning
Claim 19 depends from claim 18 (and ultimately claim 11). Claim 11 requires a "water soluble initiator containing at least one organic reactive carbonyl compound." Claim 18 enumerates exemplars: "esters, amides, carbonates, anhydrides, ketones, carbohydrates, carbamates, ureas, and hydantoins." Claim 19 as written recites "carbonic acid, or carbon dioxide in a gaseous, liquid or supercritical state." Carbonic acid/CO2 are inorganic carbonyl species, not organic reactive carbonyl compounds as required by claim 11/18. A claim in dependent form must incorporate all limitations of the claim upon which it depends and additionally limit that subject matter. Because claim 19 fails to incorporate and further limit the organic-reactive-carbonyl limitation, it is in improper dependent form. See 35 U.S.C. 112(d) (pre-AIA 4th paragraph). The Examiner therefore maintains the 35 U.S.C. 112(d) rejection for claim 19.
2. Guidance to Applicant
To place claim 19 in proper form, Applicant must do one of the following: (a) amend claim 19 so that it properly depends from claim 18 by reciting an initiator that is an organic reactive carbonyl (for example: "The method of claim 18, wherein the at least one reactive carbonyl compound is propylene carbonate"), (b) cancel claim 19, or (c) rewrite claim 19 in independent form directed specifically to carbonic acid/CO2 initiators and remove its dependency on claim 18/11. If Applicant chooses (c), the Examiner will treat the new independent claim as a new ground for search/examination.
C. Anticipation (pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)) — Claims 1–7 and 19
1. Grounds and reasoning
The Examiner maintains the rejection that claims 1–7 and 19 are anticipated by Hutchins (U.S. Pat. No. 5,268,112). Hutchins discloses mixing aqueous gel-forming ingredients including silicates and polymeric gel formers together with delayed-acting substances (esters, anhydrides) and/or gaseous precursors and placing the resultant materials into subterranean formations to alter pore-occupancy and reduce permeability. The Hutchins disclosure (as cited in the prior action) specifically teaches the use of esters and anhydrides as delay agents and also teaches injecting gellable compositions into a subterranean formation to occupy pores and reduce permeability. Those teachings read on the broad, generic limitations recited in claims 1–7 and 19, such as providing a ratio of a water soluble silicate, providing a water-dispersible polymer, providing a delayed initiator (esters/anhydrides), combining and placing into the formation to modify permeability. The Examiner therefore finds Hutchins to be anticipatory of the broad claim language now before the Office.
2. Response to Applicant's arguments
Applicant argues Hutchins is gas-generating and uses crosslinked polymers, while Applicant's claimed invention uses non-crosslinked polymers to plug and seal flow channels. Two points warrant emphasis: (a) Hutchins’ disclosure is broad and describes ‘‘gel-forming ingredient[s]’’ and includes silicates and polymeric materials as gel-formers; the cited Hutchins passages support a reading that the reference teaches forming gellable compositions employing silicates and polymeric ingredients together with esters/anhydrides/delayed agents and placing same in formations to affect pore occupancy; (b) Applicant’s claims, as presently drafted, do not contain a structural limitation that excludes the materials and approaches described in Hutchins — e.g., claim 1 and claim 11 do not require a specific, measurable non-crosslinked polymer architecture or exclude the presence of gas precursors or crosslinking mechanisms. Where claim language is broad and reads on the prior art disclosure, a rejection stands unless claim language is amended to recite distinguishing features not disclosed in the cited reference or persuasive evidence is submitted that demonstrates that the prior art does not, in fact, disclose the claimed subject matter. Applicant’s field data and declaration have been considered but do not, without further detail, rebut the prima facie case of anticipation given the breadth of the claims and the express teachings in Hutchins.
D. Obviousness (pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a)) — Claims 11–18
1. Grounds and reasoning
Claims 11–18 are rejected as obvious over Hutchins. Hutchins teaches the same set of components and the concept of delivering gel-forming species and delayed-acting agents into subterranean formations. Hutchins also suggests choices among gel reagents and delay agents, and the use of gas or delayed reagents in formation treatments. Where Hutchins does not explicitly recite the particular order of injecting a first portion of initiator, then the composition, then a second portion of initiator, established precedent treats the selection of order of process steps or mixing as prima facie obvious absent demonstration of new or unexpected results arising from the particular ordering. See In re Burhans and In re Gibson (cited in the prior action). The Examiner therefore maintains the 103 rejections for claims 11–18 in view of Hutchins and the lack of persuasive comparative evidence showing an unexpected effect arising from the claimed ordering.
2. Response to Applicant's argument regarding non-crosslinked polymers and comparative field data
Applicant argues the claimed non-crosslinked polymers yield superior, unexpected results and submitted a declaration plus a field-plot comparing two SPI treatments (non-crosslinked system) versus a Marcit (crosslinked) treatment. The Examiner has reviewed the submission. To overcome a prima facie obviousness rejection on the basis of unexpected results, Applicant must present persuasive, well-documented comparative data that (a) compares the claimed invention and the closest prior-art alternative under substantially the same conditions, (b) shows that the advantages are due to the claimed distinguishing feature(s) (here, non-crosslinked polymer usage), and (c) that the observed advantage is commensurate in scope with the claims. The submitted field plot and declaration, as currently in the record, do not supply sufficient experimental detail (e.g., exact formulations, volumes injected, pre-treatment and post-treatment test procedures, reservoir and completion specifics, statistical analysis) to permit the Examiner to find the unexpected results are attributable to the claimed limitation and are broadly representative of the claim scope. Consequently, the Examiner finds the declaration/plot insufficient to rebut the prima facie case of obviousness.
E. What Applicant can do to place the application in condition for allowance
To overcome the outstanding rejections, Applicant may pursue one or more of the following paths (not all are required; choices depend on Applicant’s prosecution strategy):
1. Amend claims to recite clear, limiting features that distinguish over Hutchins and other cited art. Examples of limiting language that might be effective include: (a) explicitly reciting "non-crosslinked" and further reciting a measurable property or preparation technique that excludes crosslinked systems (e.g., "non-crosslinked water-dispersible polymer having no covalent interchain crosslinks and with a solution intrinsic viscosity within X–Y"), (b) excluding gas precursors or gas-generation chemistries (if Applicant’s invention does not use such chemicals), or (c) reciting a specific initiator class (e.g., propylene carbonate, glyoxal) that is not disclosed by Hutchins in the claimed combination. Any new independent claim introduced will be searched and examined anew.
2. Provide persuasive, corroborated experimental evidence and a supporting sworn declaration (37 C.F.R. 1.132) that: (a) specifies the exact formulations and concentrations used for the Applicant treatment(s) and the comparative prior-art treatment(s); (b) describes the test/field procedures in detail, including reservoir conditions, injection volumes, rates, temperatures, and monitoring methods; (c) demonstrates that the observed performance advantage is due to the claimed structural limitation (for example a direct head-to-head comparison where the only difference is the non-crosslinked vs crosslinked polymer, all else held constant); and (d) shows the improvement is statistically significant and commensurate with the claim scope. Merely asserting superiority, or presenting a plot without sufficient experimental detail and controlling for confounding variables, is insufficient to overcome the Examiner's findings.
3. Cancel or properly re-draft claim 19 so that it is in proper dependent form or in independent form if carbonic acid/CO2 initiators are desired.
F. Procedural posture — continued finality
As noted in the Examiner’s June 10, 2016 action, the restriction requirement and the prior rejections were made final. Applicant’s subsequent amendment and remarks have not placed the application in condition for allowance. Accordingly, the Examiner maintains the outstanding rejections and enters this continued-final position. If Applicant files a reply that introduces new claim language or substantial new evidence (for example, a properly detailed sworn declaration with head-to-head comparative tests), the Examiner will consider whether action reopening or withdrawal of finality is appropriate and whether a supplemental search is required.
G. Summary of required applicant response
1. For claim 19: amend claim 19 to be in proper dependent form (or cancel or re-write it as independent), or follow the Examiner’s guidance above. 35 U.S.C. 112(d) rejection will be maintained until corrected.
2. For claims 1–7 and 11–18: either (a) amend the claims to include distinguishing limitations that avoid the teachings of Hutchins, or (b) submit persuasive, corroborated comparative data and a supporting sworn declaration that meets the criteria set forth above and demonstrates unexpected results commensurate with the claim scope.
3. If Applicant files amended independent claims with new subject matter, note that a supplemental search and examination may be required; fees for new claims may apply.
H. Miscellaneous
If Applicant wishes to discuss this action telephonically, call the Examiner at the telephone number listed on the file; if unreachable, the Examiner’s Supervisor contact is listed in the file wrapper. Please be specific in any telephone call so the Examiner can be prepared and so that prosecution will be efficient.
Respectfully submitted,
Examiner, Art Unit 1768
I. Limitations
[1] The Examiner relied on Hutchins (U.S. Pat. No. 5,268,112) as the primary prior art for anticipation and obviousness. If Applicant believes a different interpretation of Hutchins is warranted, Applicant must point to the exact Hutchins passages and the exact claim limitation that they contend Hutchins does not disclose.
[2] The Examiner found Applicant’s declaration and field plot to be insufficient as presented. The record lacks detailed comparative experimental procedures and compositional specifics required to support an unexpected-results showing that is commensurate in scope with the claims. Applicant may supply such evidence with a proper sworn declaration and detailed experimental data.

If Applicant demonstrates that "carbonic acid/CO2" is reasonably and inherently encompassed by the prior recited genus in claim 11/18 (with supporting arguments and evidence), the Examiner will reconsider.

Examiner Response to Applicant's A1 (Amendment and Remarks)
Summary
- The applicant filed amended claims (A1 document ISS0O53CRXEAPX3) and arguments (ISS0O53DRXEAPX3) in response to the Office action mailed May 5, 2016 (INUFX76HRXEAPX2). The applicant's amendments recite in claims 1-4 that the magnet is a 'toroidally wound magnet.' Applicant argues the cited prior art (MIT, Young, Kobayashi) do not disclose the specific radial/within-pancake conductor-width or plate strand-spacing features alleged in the claims and therefore the prior rejections should be withdrawn.
- After review of the record (including the May 5, 2016 Office action and the A1 amendment and remarks filed September 6, 2016), the examiner maintains the rejections set forth in the May 5, 2016 Office action and provides the following explanation and guidance. The application remains under active examination; the current action is non-final and the applicant is invited to reply.
Discussion of Applicant Amendments and Arguments
1) Claims 1 and 5 — 35 U.S.C. 102 (anticipated by MIT (WO 2013/180802))
- Applicant amended claim 1 to require a 'toroidally wound magnet.' The May 5, 2016 Office action relied on MIT to teach epitaxially deposited YBCO/ReBCO tapes and multi-width tape embodiments that result in a relatively constant operating-current-to-critical-current margin across a coil assembly. O1 expressly cited MIT as the anticipation basis for claims 1 and 5 (INUFX76HRXEAPX2: "Claims 1 and 5 rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1)/(a)(2) as being anticipated by MIT (WO 2013/180802).").
- Applicant's principal argument is that MIT varies tape widths between separate pancakes in an axial stack (i.e., different pancakes in the stack have different constant tape widths) and does not teach varying tape width radially within a single pancake/turn. Applicant contends MIT teaches away from within-pancake width variation and that the present disclosure instead requires radial-within-a-turn variation to maintain a relatively constant margin throughout an individual coil.
- Examiner response: The amendment narrowing the claim to a 'toroidally wound magnet' does not, on the face of the present record, remove the examiner's basis for the prior anticipation finding because O1 relied upon MIT's multi-width conductor teachings and also identified toroidal magnet embodiments in the applied art (see O1 combination references). The O1 rejection remains supported by the record citations in INUFX76HRXEAPX2. If applicant wishes to pursue a clear distinction over MIT based on the asserted intra-pancake radial-width limitation, applicant should (a) point to the precise passages in the specification that explicitly support radial-within-a-turn tape-width variation and (b) consider further amending the claims to expressly recite the intra-pancake/radial-within-a-turn limitation (for example, language to the effect of 'wherein the width of each conductor tape is varied along a single turn from an inner radial position to an outer radial position within the same coil') so the examiner and the record can unambiguously evaluate whether MIT (or other art on the record) discloses or suggests that precise limitation. Absent an amendment or persuasive record evidence that MIT contains no teaching or suggestion of the specific intra-turn radial-width variation now argued by applicant, the anticipation rejection is maintained.
2) Claims 2-4, 6 — 35 U.S.C. 103 (MIT in view of Young)
- O1 rejected these dependent claims as obvious over MIT in view of Young (INUFX76HRXEAPX2). Applicant argues Young addresses structural supports/plates but does not teach conductor arrangement required to create a uniform field in a toroid or radial-within-a-turn grading.
- Examiner response: The combination relied upon in O1 pairs the conductor-width/gradings concepts of MIT with the toroidal plates/shells/support teachings in Young to address the 'toroidally wound' limitations of the amended claims. On the current record, the combination of references remains an appropriate basis for the asserted obviousness rejection of the amended claims because the amended language (specifying a toroidal magnet) is within the scope of the toroidal teachings cited by O1 and MIT supplies the conductor-grading teachings asserted to be at issue. If applicant can (i) identify explicit specification passages that demonstrate the claimed radial-within-a-turn conductor-width variation, and (ii) either amend claims to recite that precise feature or provide persuasive arguments and evidence why the combined prior art fails to suggest the claimed structure, the examiner will re-evaluate the obviousness findings.
3) Claims 7-9 — 35 U.S.C. 103 (Young in view of MIT)
- O1 rejected these claims as obvious over Young in view of MIT. Applicant contends MIT varies widths between pancakes and does not disclose adjusting radial distance between strands in plates as recited in claim 7.
- Examiner response: The prior rejection combined Young's plate/shell toroidal teachings and MIT's conductor arrangement/optimization teachings. On the current record the examiner finds the applied combination addresses the elements recited in claims 7-9. If applicant believes 'adjusting radial distance between superconductor strands or cables in the plates' requires a structural or positional feature not taught or suggested by the applied combination, applicant should (a) supply the specific disclosure support in the present specification for that precise plate-level strand-spacing limitation and (b) consider claim language clarification (for example explicitly stating that discrete strands within a single plate are spaced non-uniformly along the plate radius to effect field uniformity). Clearer claim language and identification of supporting specification text will permit a re-assessment of the applied references against the clarified limitation.
4) Claim 10 — 35 U.S.C. 102 (anticipated by Kobayashi)
- O1 found Kobayashi anticipates the hybrid magnet having shells and radial plates, and cited Kobayashi's description of radial field variation. Applicant argues Kobayashi shows 1/r variation and does not teach providing radial-plate currents that maintain a near-constant magnetic field in the bore.
- Examiner response: O1 relied on Kobayashi to supply the shell/plate toroidal structure. The anticipation finding in O1 stands on the record citations. Applicant's argument that Kobayashi shows 1/r variation and not a near-constant bore field is recorded and will be considered. If applicant can demonstrate with record citations that Kobayashi (or any other applied reference) cannot be read to disclose the claimed radial-plate-current arrangement 'required to maintain a near-constant magnetic field' (or alternatively, if applicant amends claim 10 to more narrowly and explicitly define the required current distribution or plate configuration), the examiner will re-evaluate the anticipation conclusion. As of this action, the anticipation rejection is maintained.
Guidance to Applicant
- To overcome the rejections presently maintained, applicant may consider one or more of the following actions:
  a) Amend claims to more precisely recite the structural and functional limitations applicant relies upon as distinguishing over the applied art. Example narrowing language would explicitly state that tape width varies 'along an individual turn' from an inner radial position to an outer radial position within the same pancake or coil, or that radial plate strand spacing is varied 'within a single plate' along its radial extent to achieve the claimed near-constant bore field. Clear, unambiguous claim language tailored to the asserted distinguishing features will allow a focused re-examination of the cited references.
  b) Submit a claim-chart style response identifying the exact passages in the specification that support any newly-emphasized limitation and explain why the cited prior art does not disclose or suggest that limitation. Cite specific paragraphs/figures for each asserted distinguishing point.
  c) If applicant believes any of the cited references have been mischaracterized in O1, point to the exact passages in the applied reference establishing the correct teaching and explain why the prior characterization is incorrect.
  d) Provide affidavit or declaration (evidence) showing non-analogousness or unexpected technical effects not taught or suggested by the applied references if such evidence is available and appropriate under the statutes and rules.
Next steps
- The prior Office action rejections (May 5, 2016) are maintained as to the claims identified in this action. This communication is non-final. The applicant is invited to reply to the maintained rejections by amendment and/or argument and to provide any evidence the applicant wishes the record to consider. The examiner will reconsider the rejections in light of any new claim language, arguments, or evidence submitted by applicant.
Limitation and record note
- The examiner's maintained positions are based on the Office action of May 5, 2016 (INUFX76HRXEAPX2) and the applicant's A1 submission (ISS0O53CRXEAPX3 and ISS0O53DRXEAPX3). The entry status of the A1 claims into the official claim record is not confirmed by a subsequent Office action in the record up to the present cutoff; however, the examiner has evaluated the amended claim wording as presented in the A1. If applicant wishes to ensure specific proposed claim language is entered for examination, applicant should confirm entry procedures and, where appropriate, provide marked-up claim sets conforming to the rules for amendments after final or rule-based entry when required.
- If applicant believes a telephone interview would assist in clarifying claim language or evidentiary issues, the examiner is open to scheduling an interview after receiving a reply or request identifying specific points for discussion.
Conclusion
- The rejections stated in the May 5, 2016 Office action are maintained as to the claims identified above. This is a non-final action. Applicant is invited to file a response with claim amendments, detailed arguments and/or evidence as indicated above. The examiner will reconsider in view of any substantive, supported reply.
limitations: The record does not contain verbatim passages from the applied prior art (MIT, Young, Kobayashi) other than the examiner's characterizations quoted in the May 5, 2016 Office action; the examiner's maintained positions rely on those O1 characterizations.

Entry of the applicant-filed amended claims (ISS0O53CRXEAPX3) into the official claim record is not confirmed by any later Office action in the record up to the cutoff; the examiner has evaluated the amendment as submitted but applicant may need to ensure proper formal entry under the rules if entry is contested.

Examiner communication (Non-Final Continued Examination)

Summary
Applicant's Amendment filed November 11, 2014 (I2DT63PHPXXIFW3) and accompanying remarks have been considered. The earlier Office action of August 14, 2014 (HYROSEDBPXXIFW4) remains the basis for the outstanding rejections and findings. The record shows the applicant has: (1) amended multiple claims, (2) canceled several claims that previously raised issues, and (3) submitted arguments contesting the prior-art comparisons made in the August 14, 2014 action. This communication addresses the applicant's amendments and arguments and sets forth the examiner's position on outstanding issues.

1) Claim-objection and 35 U.S.C. § 112 matters
- The informal typographical objection to claim 3 in O1 is withdrawn. The claim text in the November 11, 2014 amendment corrects the misspelling; no further action is required for that informal defect. (See I2DT63PHPXXIFW3, claim 3.)

Applicant's November 11, 2014 submission cancels claims 7, 20 and 21; those cancellations render the corresponding 112(b) objections moot for the canceled claims. Claim 15 was amended to supply antecedent language and thus the 112(b) objection to claim 15 is withdrawn. (See I2DT63PHPXXIFW3, claim 15.)
- No new 112 objections are made in this communication for the currently pending claim set on the record. If future claim amendments introduce ambiguous or indefinite antecedent language or other 112 issues, new objections may be made.

2) Prior-art rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 102 and § 103 (O1 rejections maintained)
- The August 14, 2014 action rejected many of the then-pending claims as anticipated by DE 34 36 089 (Kronseder) (see HYROSEDBPXXIFW4). Those rejections are maintained as to the pending claims on the record that correspond to the subject matter addressed by O1. Specifically, claims asserted in O1 to be anticipated or obvious over Kronseder remain rejected for the reasons summarized in O1 unless and until applicant submits persuasive documentary evidence or claim amendments that distinguish over the reference.
- Applicant's November 11, 2014 remarks argue that Kronseder's embodiments use a solid metal bar or rigid plastic for the support member and ceramic sliding elements, and that Kronseder's machines are labeling machines rather than 'cleaning systems.' Applicant also contends Kronseder's sliding elements are fixed with an adhesive and therefore not 'individually exchangeable.' These are factual contentions about the content of the reference. The examiner notes: the O1 action already identified structural elements in Kronseder (supporting member with recess/groove, sliding/slide elements, anchoring points, fastenings, plurality/butt-joint arrangement, grooves providing a flush upper surface in certain embodiments) and relied on those disclosures for the anticipation and obviousness conclusions (HYROSEDBPXXIFW4). - Consequently, the following rejections remain outstanding and are continued: claims 1-6, 10, 12-20 (as applicable to the pending claim texts) under 35 U.S.C. § 102; and claims 7-9, 11 and 21 under 35 U.S.C. § 103, consistent with O1's analyses. The O1 action is the controlling prior-art comparison on the record (HYROSEDBPXXIFW4). Applicant's arguments have been considered but are not, as presented, sufficient to overcome the prior-art comparisons made in O1.

3) How applicant may respond to advance prosecution
The applicant may overcome the outstanding rejections by one or more of the following:
- File a claim amendment that adds clear, definite structural or functional limitations not shown or suggested by Kronseder, thereby distinguishing the claims over the reference; or
- Submit documentary evidence (for example, an authenticated translation or copy of Kronseder that applicant relies upon, or an affidavit/declaration under 37 C.F.R. § 1.132) that persuasively shows the portions of Kronseder relied on in O1 do not disclose the asserted features (for example, that the support member is not a sheet-metal wall as claimed, or that the sliding elements lack the structural relationship required by the claims); or

Office Action (Non-Final) — Response to Applicant's A1 Submission
Summary
The Office has considered applicant’s Amendment and Reply filed November 26, 2014 (A1), the previously mailed non-final Office Action dated August 27, 2014 (CTNF; HZCRBTS5PXXIFW4), and the application file record. The earlier Office Action rejected claims 1–12 under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as anticipated by Takahashi (US 2006/0143418). Applicant has amended claim language (proposed claims filed with A1) and argued the cited reference does not teach two distinctions: (1) grouping storage apparatuses by their physical site, and (2) a copy-pair setting policy that explicitly includes an indicator of "local copy" versus "remote copy." The Examiner has reviewed the amendments and arguments and responds as follows.
Amendments and Procedural Status
- Applicant submitted amended claims and a specification title change in the A1. The record shows the as-filed claims from the original publication (H52R47QJPXXIFW3) remain entered. The applicant-submitted amended claims in I2YYHZE4PXXIFW3 are recorded in the file as proposed amendments with entry status unknown. The Examiner has considered the arguments in A1 but cannot treat proposed claim text as entered until formally entered under 37 C.F.R. § 1.121 (or until applicant confirms replacement of the pending claim set). Accordingly, the Examiner proceeds on the basis of the claims of record (the as-filed claims) and addresses applicant's arguments directed to Takahashi.
Substantive Response to Applicant's Arguments
- Applicant's central arguments: Applicant contends Takahashi does not disclose (A) grouping of storage apparatuses by physical site (applicant's term: "storage apparatuses disposed at an identical site are grouped as an identical storage group") and (B) a copy pair setting policy that includes explicit local/remote copy information for pairs of virtual volumes.
- Examiner analysis and determination: The August 27, 2014 Office Action applied Takahashi to claims 1–12. That action relied on Takahashi's disclosures of (i) user-definable grouping of volumes (migration groups and storage layers) and (ii) migration/copying control between volumes. The Office interpreted Takahashi's grouping by network zone or host access reports and its grouping/migration constructs as corresponding to claimed grouping functionality and the ability to effect copy/migration relationships between grouped volumes. On the present record, applicant has not shown that those interpretations are incorrect. Applicant's assertions that Takahashi is "silent" about 'site' membership and explicit local/remote copy policy are noted; however, the Examiner continues to find that Takahashi's grouping by network/zone or by host-access (host report) together with its migration control between groups reasonably correspond to the claimed grouping and copy-pair-setting concepts when read in light of the specification. The prior Office Action specifically cited Takahashi's FIG. 1, FIG. 11, and the description of grouping/migration behavior, and concluded those disclosures anticipate the claimed apparatus and method. Applicant has not pointed to a specific portion of Takahashi showing that the cited figures and description are inapposite. The record therefore supports maintaining the prior 35 U.S.C. 102(b) rejections.
Claim-specific guidance and options for applicant
- If applicant believes the Examiner’s application of Takahashi is incorrect, applicant should (i) identify precise, numbered paragraph(s) and figure(s) of Takahashi that the applicant asserts do not, in fact, disclose the particular limitation(s) (pinpoint citations), and provide explanation why those portions do not disclose the limitation(s) as applied in the Office action; and/or (ii) provide persuasive claim amendments that clearly distinguish the claim limitations from the Takahashi disclosure. For example, if a "site" limitation is intended to mean a particular physical location attribute stored and used by the management apparatus, add explicit claim language requiring a stored 'site identifier' or a specified data structure/field and identify where that support appears in the specification. Likewise, if the copy-pair setting policy must explicitly include a stored "copy-type" field indicating 'local' or 'remote', add such a limitation and cite the specification for support.
- If applicant submits amended claims, please ensure that the proposed claim set is formally entered and that any new limitations have explicit support in the specification (cite paragraph(s) or figure(s)). If applicant requests withdrawal of the pending rejection based on claim amendments, be aware that the Examiner will re-assess novelty and, if applicable, nonobviousness in view of the cited art and any art of record.
Disposition
- The pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) rejections of the pending claims 1–12 over Takahashi are maintained on the present record. This communication is a non-final action. Applicant's options include: (1) file an amendment presenting claim language that overcomes the cited Takahashi disclosure (with support citations) and request entry of the amended claims; (2) file a persuasive written argument with pinpoint citations to the Takahashi reference showing the cited portions do not disclose the claimed limitations; (3) request an interview to discuss specific claim language and the cited reference; or (4) if applicant believes Takahashi has been mischaracterized, identify the precise passages and explain the mischaracterization.
- If applicant elects to amend, include claims in a form suitable for entry and identify the support in the specification for any new or clarified limitations. If amendments are filed, the Examiner will consider them and determine whether any rejection remains appropriate in view of Takahashi and the rest of the application file.
Limitations and procedural notes

Applicant is encouraged to cite specific portions of Takahashi (by paragraph and figure) that are relied upon in prosecution to assist the Examiner in verifying the exact content of that reference.

If applicant wants the proposed claims entered and considered as the pending claims, inform the Office and provide a clean claim set in compliance with 37 C.F.R. § 1.121.
Conclusion / Next steps

If applicant elects to file an amendment, please: (a) provide a claim set in formal form for entry; (b) point to the specification support for any new limitations; and (c) if relying on prior art distinctions, provide pinpoint citations to the prior art relied upon.

However, Toshiba also teaches placing structures (features) relative to sub-pixel geometry (see pgpub_description describing dots/sub-pixel placement). The legal question for an obviousness rejection is whether a skilled artisan would have been prompted to combine the teachings of the references to arrive at the claimed arrangement. Toshiba's disclosure of per-subpixel structural variation and Hitachi's disclosure of optically-detectable dot patterns that interact with pixel regions supply a rationale to distribute marks among sub-pixels to reduce visible unevenness. That optimization — allocating more marks to sub-pixels of a color with lower luminosity to mask visible unevenness — is a predictable design choice a person of ordinary skill would make given the combined teachings. Applicant's declaration of functional difference between scanning-line segments and position marks is noted, but does not persuasively negate the combination rationale because Toshiba's teaching shows per-subpixel structural manipulation that can be applied to optically-readable mark placement. parsed.office_action:
Examiner Communication
Introduction and procedural status
This communication follows the Office's January 5, 2016 action (CTNF) in which claims 1-14 (originally filed) were rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 over Hitachi Maxell (JP 2007-133824A) in view of Toshiba Mobile Display (JP 2010-060996A). Applicant's April 5, 2016 response cancels claims 1-14 and submits new claims 15-34 (amendment IMNS5HH3PXXIFW3) together with arguments (remarks IMNS5HH9PXXIFW3). Claims 15 and 32 are the independent claims added by Applicant.
Summary of Examiner position
- Claims 1-14: moot because Applicant cancelled them.
- New claims 15 and 32 (independents): the Examiner maintains that the combination of the prior art references Hitachi Maxell and Toshiba Mobile Display renders the claimed subject matter obvious under 35 U.S.C. 103. Dependent claims 16-31 and 33-34 rise or fall with independents 15 and 32 and are treated below.
Grounds and reasoning (35 U.S.C. 103)
1) Mapping of claimed elements to prior art
- Display device/display region, pixels, and optically readable position patterns/marks: Hitachi discloses a display device and dot patterns that encode position information and are optically read by a pen/reader. The specification describes dot patterns/dots used to obtain coordinates (pgpub_description: "the dot pattern is an example of a position information pattern" and "the dot patterns are made of a material that absorbs infrared light").
- Pixel and sub-pixel structure (colored sub-pixels): Toshiba discloses pixel structures with sub-pixels of different colors and describes structural elements associated with sub-pixel regions (IIUAYJKCPXXIFW4; pgpub_claims; pgpub_description and figures of the published application illustrate per-subpixel geometry).
- Distribution/placement of marks among sub-pixels: the combined teachings of Hitachi and Toshiba disclose both optically-detectable marks and per-subpixel structural manipulation. A person of ordinary skill would reasonably combine these teachings to locate optically-readable marks in relation to sub-pixel structure to improve pen-readability while reducing visible display non-uniformity.
2) Motivation to combine and predictable result
- The references are analogous: both concern display technology and the use of display-surface features to enable optical reading/input. Toshiba's teaching of sub-pixel-related structures provides motivation to consider mark placement with awareness of sub-pixel color/luminosity. Hitachi's teaching about how dots interact with display optics (including reflections/infrared absorption) provides the practical technique for optically encoding local position. Combining these disclosures to alter the distribution of marks among sub-pixels to reduce visible unevenness (for example, placing more marks in sub-pixels of a color having lower luminosity) is a design choice that yields predictable results to a skilled artisan.
3) Specific claim limitations and Examiner view
- Claims 15 and 32: recite that a total number of position marks in first pixels (lower luminosity) is greater than in second pixels (higher luminosity). Toshiba and Hitachi together teach per-subpixel placement of marks and the optical behavior of marks; applying the known desire to reduce visible unevenness, a skilled artisan would have been motivated to allocate marks to less visually conspicuous sub-pixels (i.e., lower-luminosity colors). Thus the claimed numeric inequality would have been an obvious optimization.
- Claim 22 (position mark disposed in a light transparent portion inside a pixel): Applicant argues Hitachi teaches dot placement between pixels to avoid interference and thus opposes placing marks inside pixels. Examiner notes Toshiba's disclosure of sub-pixel-associated structures and concludes that Toshiba provides motivation/teaching to place structures associated with sub-pixel regions, including transmissive portions within a pixel. Therefore, placing a mark within a transmissive portion is a foreseeable design alternative and is an obvious variation when combining the disclosures.
Applicant's arguments and Examiner response
Applicant contends that Toshiba's 'segments' are scanning-line structures distinct from Hitachi's position marks and do not teach allocating marks preferentially to particular sub-pixel colors; Applicant argues there is no motivation to alter Hitachi's marks distribution. The Examiner acknowledges the structural differences but finds that Toshiba nonetheless teaches per-subpixel structural manipulation and positioning relative to sub-pixel geometry. That feature supplies a motivation to vary mark placement/distribution in a display that also uses optically-detectable marks (Hitachi). The combination of teachings gives the skilled artisan a reason to place marks so as to reduce visible unevenness, including biasing mark counts toward lower-luminosity sub-pixels. Applicant's point about Hitachi's preferred inter-pixel placement to avoid optical interference is noted, but the Examiner finds Toshiba's per-subpixel teachings supply a credible alternative placement rationale.
Disposition and next steps
- The Examiner maintains the rejection of the independent claims 15 and 32 and their dependent claims under 35 U.S.C. 103 over Hitachi Maxell in view of Toshiba Mobile Display for the reasons set forth above.
- The Applicant is given opportunity to reply further. To traverse the maintained 103 rejection, Applicant may: (a) amend claims to recite additional structural or functional limitations not taught or suggested by the applied references; or (b) present persuasive objective evidence and/or technical reasoning (e.g., declaration by a qualified person) showing that the cited combination is unsound, that the cited references teach away from the combination, or that the particular arrangement yields unexpected results beyond predictable design choice. Applicant may also request an examiner interview to discuss claim language and possible amendment paths to allowance.
Claim status summary
- Claims 1-14: cancelled; original 103 rejection moot.
- Claims 15-34: pending and rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as unpatentable over Hitachi Maxell (JP 2007-133824A) in view of Toshiba Mobile Display (JP 2010-060996A). The Examiner maintains the rejection for the reasons stated.
References relied upon (as in prior action)
- JP 2007-133824 A (Hitachi Maxell) (discloses ink/dot patterns and optically-readable dot patterns in a display and teaches that dot patterns are made of infrared-absorbing material; see pgpub_description: "the dot patterns are made of a material that absorbs infrared light, and thus, infrared light is not reflected at the dot patterns")
- JP 2010-060996 A (Toshiba Mobile Display) (discloses per-subpixel structures and sub-pixel color arrangement; see IIUAYJKCPXXIFW4 and pgpub_claims stating "each of the pixels includes sub pixels of a plurality of different colors")
Procedural note
This is a non-final (but continued) examination communication maintaining the prior art combination rejection as applied to the newly presented claims. Applicant has not persuasively shown entitlement to allowance of claims 15-34 over the cited art in the present record. Applicant may respond by amendment and/or by providing evidence or argument as indicated above. If Applicant files an amendment that places the claims in a condition for allowance, the Examiner will consider allowance; otherwise a final action may follow upon the next appropriate opportunity.
Limitations
- The Examiner's reasoning relies on the content of the two cited Japanese patent publications listed above and Applicant's submitted specification and claims. The Examiner's assessment that Toshiba teaches per-subpixel structural variation is drawn from the references on record. If there are additional references or evidence (e.g., priority documents, declarations, or unpublished prosecution history) not of record, the Examiner has not considered them here.

If Applicant believes any procedural defect occurred in claim entry, Applicant should raise it specifically and provide supporting evidence.
Examiner contact
If Applicant wishes to discuss claim amendments or this position, an examiner interview is recommended. The Examiner can be contacted per the previous Office Action information.

RESPONSE TO APPLICANT REMARKS (A1) — SUMMARY AND FINDINGS
This communication responds to Applicant's February 16, 2017 Remarks (A1) traversing the prior-art anticipation rejections in the Office Action mailed November 16, 2016 (O1). The Examiner has considered the arguments in the Remarks and the claim language as filed. For the reasons explained below, the 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) rejections of Claims 1-3, 8, 11-13 and 18 over Tamura (US 2005/0070336 A1) are maintained. Claims 4-7, 9-10, 14-17 and 19-20 remain objected to as dependent on rejected claims but are allowable only if rewritten in independent form including the limitations of their base claims.
RESPONDING TO THE APPLICANT'S ARGUMENTS
Applicant's principal argument is that Tamura fails to teach the claimed distinction between a "first communication module" (that establishes a communication channel to an external electronic device based on wired or short-range communications) and a "second communication module" (that supports a communication service via a base station), and therefore Tamura cannot disclose a control module that "obtains a communication profile required for operating the second communication module using the external electronic device connected through the first communication module." Applicant asserts Tamura only discloses a single mobile station and not two separate modules operating as in the claim.
Examiner's analysis and response
1) Functional claim language and the disclosure in Tamura The claims at issue are written in functional terms ("first communication module configured to establish...","second communication module that supports...", and a "control module configured to obtain..."). The Examiner construes such functional recitations to be satisfied by structures in the prior art that perform the recited functions. Tamura explicitly describes a mobile station interacting via short-range wireless procedures (Bluetooth) with a terminal device and then transmitting a data-communication resume signal so that data communication is restarted between the base station and the terminal device "through the mobile station". The Examiner relies on the Examiner's Office Action record citation of Tamura (O1). The O1 action quotes Tamura describing Bluetooth-based session establishment and the mobile station relaying/resuming data communication with a base station. See the record text relied on in the O1 action: "Then, the mobile station 2 (server) and the terminal device 3 (client) perform processing of transmission/reception of a data service connection request S37, transmission/reception of a response signal S38 and a session establishment S39 based on the Bluetooth standard procedure, thereby achieving the data communication in the BWC." and "When this data communication is achieved, the mobile station 2 transmits a data communication resume signal to the base station 1 (S40). As a result, the data communication S41 is restarted between the base station 1 and the terminal device 3 through the mobile station 2." The Examiner's view is that Tamura discloses the functional arrangement recited in the claims: a device with a short-range interface used to establish a connection to an external device and a base-station interface used to effect a base-station communication, and control/session behavior that relays and resumes communication between the terminal and base station via the mobile station. The Examiner therefore finds Tamura anticipates the functional elements recited in Claims 1 and 11, and the related dependent elements recited in the rejected claims.
2) Applicant's contention regarding physically distinct modules Applicant appears to argue the claims require a particular physical separation or architectural distinction between the two modules that Tamura does not teach. The present claims do not expressly recite a requirement that the two modules be separate physical devices or separate ICs; rather the claims recite modules by function. Under established examination practice, if Applicant requires a stricter physical/structural limitation (for example, "a first transceiver distinct from a second transceiver" or explicitly separate hardware elements), Applicant must amend the claims to include those limitations. If Applicant files amended claims including structural limitations that are not met by Tamura, the Examiner will re-evaluate the prior art with respect to the amended claims.
3) Dependent claims and claims the Examiner found allowable in O1 The Examiner's prior Office Action explicitly stated that Claims 4-7, 9-10, 14-17 and 19-20 are objected to as depending from rejected claims but would be allowable if rewritten in independent form including their base claim limitations. The Applicant's Remarks acknowledges the Examiner found these claims allowable. That finding stands: those particular claims remain dependent on rejected claims and thus cannot be allowed in the present claim set unless rewritten appropriately.
DECISION — MAINTENANCE OF 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) REJECTIONS
For the reasons above, the Examiner maintains the 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) rejections of Claims 1-3, 8, 11-13 and 18 over Tamura. The Examiner finds Tamura discloses the claimed functional elements for the reasons set forth above and as supported by the record text quoted in the prior Office Action.
APPLICANT OPTIONS
1) Amend the claims If Applicant wishes to traverse the rejection on the ground that the claims should require structural features not found in Tamura, amend the claims to add those structural limitations (for example, explicitly recite physically distinct transceivers, or add structural detail about a separate provisioning/profile manager component). Claims amended to include structural limitations that are not met by Tamura will be examined afresh against the applied prior art and any other art of record. If amendments are made, please provide remarks explaining how the amended language changes claim scope and how the amended claims distinguish over Tamura and other cited art.
2) Request interview The Examiner is available for an interview to discuss claim scope, claim amendment language, or other matters. Applicant may request an interview; if desired please propose times/dates and the proposed attendees. The Examiner can be contacted as noted in the prior Office Action.
3) File persuasive reply/evidence If Applicant believes there is a factual error in the Examiner's reading of Tamura or can point to specific portions of Tamura (with full citations to the reference text) that show the Examiner's characterization is incorrect, Applicant may submit a reply with argument and/or supporting evidence. Note that a bare assertion that Tamura lacks the claimed functions without amendment of the claims to add the structural limitation Applicant seeks is not persuasive where the claims are functional in scope and the reference discloses the same functions.
LIMITATIONS
- The Examiner's maintained rejections rely on the characterization of Tamura set forth in the earlier Office Action (CTNF O1). The record contains the Examiner's quotations of Tamura (see O1). The complete Tamura publication text is not reproduced in full in the present record documents available in the application file; the Examiner relied on the cited passages set out in the prior Office Action. If Applicant submits the full Tamura reference showing different language or context, the Examiner will consider it.
- If Applicant files amended claims or submits additional evidence/arguments, the Examiner will consider them and, as appropriate, may enter new or amended grounds of rejection or may allow claims that are patentable over the cited art.
CONCLUSION
The Examiner maintains the 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) rejections of Claims 1-3, 8, 11-13 and 18 over Tamura for the reasons above. Applicant may respond by filing claim amendments, affidavits/arguments, or requesting an interview. If Applicant elects to amend, please include claim remarks explaining how the amendments overcome the applied references.
Examiner contact information is provided in the prior Office Action. The Examiner is available for telephone interview as requested.
(End of communication)

Examiner Action (Non-Final) — Substantive Response to Applicant's Amendment and Remarks
Summary
- Admissions and changes: Applicant amended claims 1–4 and 6. The amendment adding “at least one processor to implement:” to claim 1 is acknowledged. Applicant added a “starting point” and recited that buttons are spaced apart from that starting point in the character pad interface. Applicant provided remarks requesting withdrawal of certain formal objections and argued that the cited references do not disclose the claimed features.
- Examiner determinations: The earlier rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (interpretation under the sixth paragraph) and certain 35 U.S.C. 112(b) objections are withdrawn in view of Applicant’s amendments. The prior art rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102 (Shin) and 35 U.S.C. 103 (Kornev) are maintained for the reasons below.
Detailed Findings and Action
1) 35 U.S.C. 112(f) / claim-interpretation objection — WITHDRAWN as to claims 1–3
- Background: In the January 20, 2017 Office action the Examiner held that limitations reciting a "gesture recognition unit" and "control unit" invoked 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph) because they used a generic placeholder ("unit") with functional language and lacked sufficient structure. The Office action requested identification of corresponding structure in the specification or amendment to avoid application of 112(f).
- Applicant's amendment: Independent claim 1 was amended to recite "at least one processor to implement:" prior to the gesture recognizer and controller functional recitations (J1HXC0SNRXEAPX5). Applicant relied on that amendment to rebut the 112(f) interpretation.
- Examiner response: The recitation of a structural entity "at least one processor" that implements the recited functions provides a concrete structural basis sufficient to withdraw the prior 112(f) interpretation for the current claim set. Therefore the 112(f) interpretational rejection (and the associated requirement to point to corresponding structure in the specification for the previously-protested generic "unit" terms) is withdrawn for claims 1–3 as currently amended.
2) 35 U.S.C. 112(b) / cooperative-relationship objections — WITHDRAWN as to claims 3 and 6
- Background: The previous Office action found claims 3 and 6 incomplete for omitting the positional/cooperative relationship between the "reference position" and the "button of the character pad" (i.e., whether the reference position is inside or outside a button). The Examiner identified specification paragraphs [0051]-[0055] as showing the reference position inside a button.
- Applicant's amendment: Claims 3 and 6 were amended to state that the character pad interface comprises a plurality of buttons spaced apart from the starting point located in the central area of the character pad interface, and the dragging is from the starting point (J1HXC0SNRXEAPX5). This language supplies the positional/cooperative relationship previously identified as missing.
- Examiner response: The amendment supplies the necessary positional relationship, and the previously issued 112(b) cooperative-relationship objection for claims 3 and 6 is withdrawn.
3) 35 U.S.C. 102 — ANTICIPATION BY Shin (KR 2010/0064899) — MAINTAINED for claims 1–6
- Prior Examiner analysis (January 20, 2017) characterized Shin as teaching a touch-screen input object with characters arranged around the input object and a drag/select/release operation that results in character recognition (IY3AQZKSRXEAPX5, paragraph summarizing Shin). The Examiner previously noted Shin's figures and description as teaching an input object with an initial/reference position and character groups corresponding to drag directions; release after drag causes selection/recognition of the character.
- Applicant's argument: Applicant contends Shin does not disclose a character pad that "comprises a character pad interface in which a starting point indicating a type of characteristics that is enabled to be input through a currently activated interface is positioned in a central area of the character pad interface," and therefore the anticipation should be withdrawn.
- Examiner analysis and conclusion: The Applicant's amendment narrows claim 1 to recite a starting point centrally located in the character pad interface and that buttons are spaced apart from that starting point. However, Shin's disclosure of a touch-screen input object with characters arranged around the input object, combined with the described drag selection and release behavior, reasonably reads on a character pad that has a central starting region (input object) and selectable groups around it. The Examiner's prior characterization of Shin supports reading Shin as disclosing an input object with surrounding character groups and selection by drag direction back-to-release. On the present record and considering Applicant's arguments, the Examiner finds Shin to disclose or inherently teach the features recited in the claims and therefore maintains the anticipation rejection for claims 1–6.
- Applicant action suggested: If Applicant believes Shin lacks the recited central starting point or that Shin's structure/operation is meaningfully different, Applicant should (a) identify specific Shin passages and figures that show a contrary structure or operation and explain why those differences are dispositive, or (b) propose further claim amendments to recite additional structural or functional features not present in Shin.
4) 35 U.S.C. 103 — Kornev et al. (US 2010/0333011) — MAINTAINED for claims 1–2 and 4–5
- Prior Examiner analysis: The Office action explained that Kornev teaches multi-character selection via sliding gestures and character menus and that it would have been obvious to modify Kornev's four-corner selection to an eight-group arrangement like the claimed one, such that horizontal, vertical and diagonal slide gestures are recognized (IY3AQZKSRXEAPX5). The Examiner provided a rationale: reducing the number of keys on small touch screens motivates arranging more characters per key and using slide gestures in additional directions to select among them.
- Applicant's argument: Applicant traversed the rejection and emphasized the added central starting point limitation in claim 1.
- Examiner response: The Examiner maintains that substituting or adapting Kornev's multi-character key arrangement to an eight-character-group arrangement and applying the same slide-selection technique yields the claimed recognition of horizontal, vertical, and diagonal gestures and that displaying the selected character as confirmation is within Kornev's teaching. Therefore the obviousness rejection over Kornev is maintained for claims 1–2 and 4–5 on the present record.
- Applicant action suggested: Applicant may (a) point to specific, annotated portions of Kornev that they contend do not disclose or suggest the claimed central starting point or other claim limitations, (b) further amend the claims to add limitations not present in Kornev (for example, particular processor operations, temporal ordering, GUI behavior or labeling), or (c) provide persuasive evidence (e.g., expert declaration, contemporaneous industry documents) that the combination would not have been made for the reasons asserted by the Examiner.
Summary of Examiner disposition
- Withdrawn: 35 U.S.C. 112(f) interpretation objection (for claims 1–3) and the cooperative-relationship 35 U.S.C. 112(b) objection for claims 3 and 6 have been withdrawn in view of Applicant's amendments.
- Maintained: Prior art rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102 (Shin) and 35 U.S.C. 103 (Kornev) are maintained for the claims indicated above. The Examiner has relied on the prior office action analysis and the record statements identifying how the cited references teach the claimed concept of a central input region and surrounding selectable character groups chosen by horizontal/vertical/diagonal drag gestures.
Next steps available to Applicant
- Amend the claims to further distinguish from Shin and/or Kornev (e.g., add specific processor-implemented steps, GUI element identifiers, temporal confirmation behaviors, or other structural limitations not found in the cited references),
- Submit a reply arguing why the cited references do not disclose or suggest the claimed features with precise line/figure citations to the references, or
- File evidence (e.g., annotated prior art, declarations) that supports non-anticipation or non-obviousness.
Limitations and record notes
- The Examiner relied on the previously-issued January 20, 2017 Office action for the primary prior-art and 112 analyses. Applicant's amendment adding "at least one processor" is credited and led to withdrawal of the 112(f) interpretational ground. The Examiner's maintenance of the 102/103 rejections is based on the Examiner's prior characterization of Shin and Kornev as found in the record (IY3AQZKSRXEAPX5). If Applicant provides pinpointed citation-based argumentation or further amendments, the Examiner will reconsider those in the next Office action.
Conclusion
Claims 1–6 remain pending. Applicant's amendments cured the earlier 112 procedural/interpretation defects identified in the January 20, 2017 action; those objections are withdrawn. However, the prior art rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 35 U.S.C. 103 remain. Applicant is invited to respond by amendment and/or argument addressing the maintained rejections. The Examiner is amenable to an interview to discuss claim amendments and the cited references.

Examiner Action (Non-Final) - Summary and Reasons for Action
Summary
The Office action mailed January 5, 2015 (CTNF) rejected claims 1–19 under 35 U.S.C. 103 and rejected claims 9 and 15 under 35 U.S.C. 112(b). Applicant's reply filed February 27, 2015 amended claims 9 and 15 and traversed the § 103 rejections and the § 112 rejection. Applicant also confirmed election of the process invention (claims 1–19). The amendment to claims 9 and 15 as entered in the record contains unclear/garbled wording and therefore does not cure the previous 112(b) objection. The § 103 rejections are maintained as to the recited claims for the reasons set forth below. This action is non-final; applicant may respond by amendment and/or by persuasive argument or by submission of evidence in support of patentability.
Claims under Consideration / Current Claim Scope
- Entered claim set: claims 1–19 entered as originally filed; claim 20 withdrawn (elected process invention I was confirmed by applicant). Applicant's A1 proposed amendments for claims 9 and 15 were filed but the text as recorded in the file is unclear. The Examiner treats the recorded amendment as unclear for examination purposes and requests clarification.
Substantive Examination — 35 U.S.C. 112(b)
- Status: maintained for claims 9 and 15.
- Reason: The initial Office action identified ambiguity of the term 'low fluorine tungsten.' Applicant amended claims 9 and 15 to avoid 'low fluorine' language. However, the amended claim language as entered in the file is not intelligible (e.g., 'new-fte-iie tungsten' and '4*eva ie- tungsten by a levfucrine-tungsten process'), such that the Examiner cannot determine claim scope. Under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention. Applicant must present clear, conventional claim language. Please submit corrected claims 9 and 15 that unambiguously recite the intended limitation. Suggested clear phrasing (if consistent with applicant intent and supported by the specification) is: 'The method of claim X wherein depositing metal in the trench ... comprises depositing low-fluorine tungsten by a chemical vapor deposition process in which fluorine concentration at the deposition interface is controlled.' If applicant intends alternative terminology or a specific numerical fluorine concentration, please state it and identify corresponding support in the specification.
Substantive Examination — 35 U.S.C. 103
- Status: maintained (non-final) for claims 1–7, 8, 10–19 as previously rejected.
- Reason (overview): The Examiner's prior analysis combining Choi (US 2014/0179093 A1), Lin (US 2014/0264911 A1), and Cheng (US 2011/0287600 A1) provides articulated reasons with supporting passages for why the claimed limitations would have been obvious. Choi provides the replacement-gate structure, metal fill (including tungsten), and liner context. Lin teaches removal of excess conductive material by planarizing and states such planarizing 'may also be performed with etch-back techniques' and that the planarizing process may 'stop on the polish stop layer.' Cheng demonstrates that selective etch-back chemistries can remove one material (e.g., epitaxial SiGe stressor) while leaving adjacent unmasked metal gate material substantially unaffected, supporting the concept that selective chemistries can be chosen to remove a particular overburden and not attack a liner or other elements. Hirano and Yamaguchi teach known CVD processes for tungsten (including nitrogen-assisted and low-fluorine WF6-based approaches), and Aoyama and Quirk-Serda teach reactive ion etch practices for gate recessing. The Examiner finds that a person of ordinary skill would have had reason to combine these teachings to achieve the claimed result and that the combination would have had a reasonable expectation of success.
- Specific points in response to applicant arguments:
  - Applicant: Lin teaches CMP and the optional mention of 'etch-back' does not mean Lin teaches a pure non-mechanical chemical overburden removal as claimed. Examiner: Lin explicitly states that the planarizing process may be performed with etch-back techniques and that the process may stop on a polish-stop layer. That disclosure supports substituting or combining etch-back removal for the overburden removal step; the skilled artisan would understand and be motivated to employ etch-back chemistries to remove excess conductive fill and stop on a liner/polish-stop if desired.
  - Applicant: Cheng etches SiGe and does not teach etching metals; Cheng's selective etch of SiGe does not demonstrate selective etching of a metal overburden. Examiner: Cheng establishes that selective chemistries and etch-back approaches can be configured to remove one material in the presence of adjacent unmasked materials; it therefore supports the general concept of selective etch-back to remove an overburden while leaving other materials substantially intact. Combined with Lin's etch-back/polish-stop teaching and Choi's gate structure, the combination provides the skilled artisan with a reasonable expectation that an appropriate selective chemistry (as further supported by other cited art for metal etch chemistries) could be used to remove a metal overburden and stop on a liner.
  - Applicant has not presented persuasive documentary evidence that would rebut the Examiner's combination rationale (such as a contemporaneous teaching-away or experimental data demonstrating that the claimed selective metal overburden removal is inoperable or was unknown); absent such evidence the Examiner maintains the prior rejections.
Action Required — How Applicant May Respond
1) Clarify claims 9 and 15: File corrected claim language that unambiguously defines the intended limitation for those claims. If a numerical range for fluorine concentration or a specific process name is intended, recite it and point to support in the specification. This is required to address the maintained 112(b) objection.
2) To traverse the § 103 rejections: submit persuasive argument and/or evidence explaining why the cited combination does not teach or suggest the claimed subject matter and/or why the combination would not have been made by a skilled artisan. Points that may be persuasive include: showing the cited references teach away from replacing CMP with an etch-back for metal overburden removal; contemporaneous art or data showing etch chemistries selective to tungsten (or other gate metals) while stopping on the recited liner were not known or were inoperative; or amending claims to recite additional limitations that distinguish over the combination (for example claim limitations identifying a specific etchant chemistry, process conditions, polish-stop material combination, or a structural limitation not taught by the cited art).
3) Amendment option: Applicant may amend claims to include additional limitations supported by the specification to avoid the cited prior art combination. If claims are amended, please provide an election statement if new claim sets implicate the prior restriction requirement.
4) Request for interview: The applicant requested a telephone interview in A1; the Examiner continues to be available. To schedule, please propose times and an agenda via the electronic file wrapper or by contacting the Examiner; confirm any proposed claim amendments prior to interview to facilitate productive discussion.
Limitations
- The record contains the Examiner's prior action (I4CTKN69PXXIFW4) and the applicant's A1 response (I6O2B534PXXIFW3, I6O2B53SPXXIFW3, I6O2B54PPXXIFW3). The A1 amendment text for claims 9 and 15 in the file as entered contains garbled wording; the Examiner has relied on the entered text and thus requests a corrected clear amendment. If applicant submits an unambiguous corrected claim set, the Examiner will reconsider the 112(b) objection in view of that corrected text.
Conclusion
- The Examiner maintains the non-final obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103) rejections for the indicated claims and maintains the 112(b) objection to claims 9 and 15 as currently entered. This action is non-final. Applicant is invited to respond by amendment and/or by submitting argument or evidence. If applicant files a clear corrected amendment to claims 9 and 15 and/or persuasive evidence or argument distinguishing the claims from the applied references, the Examiner will reconsider the rejections and may withdraw or alter them as appropriate.
