parsed.office_action:
Examiner Communication — Non-Final Action (continued prosecution)
Summary of Action
This communication follows the Office action mailed June 13, 2016 (the first action, IPPLGGCBRXEAPX1) and Applicant’s reply and amendment filed September 22, 2016 (ITEPH30NRXEAPX4; ITEPH30MRXEAPX4; ITEPH30ORXEAPX4). Applicant has (a) amended the specification and title, (b) submitted replacement Figures 4 and 5, and (c) amended and cancelled various claims per the September 22 filing. The record shows the Applicant cancelled claims 8, 9, 11 and 13; the Examiner treats those claims as withdrawn. Applicant argues that the amendments overcome the prior objections and rejections. After careful consideration of the amendments and arguments, the Examiner reaches the following determinations.
Drawings and Title
- Title: Applicant amended the title in the specification and submitted a Supplemental ADS per the A1 filing. The Examiner accepts the amended title for record purposes. (See ITEPH30MRXEAPX4: amended title text.)
- Drawings: Applicant submitted replacement Figures 4 and 5 (ITEPH30ORXEAPX4; ITG2IBLYPXXIFW2). The Examiner notes support for elements shown in the replacement figures is present in the specification (see pgpub_description/I2Y16E1MPXXIFW3). However the earlier Office action objected to missing axis labels on Figures 1, 2b, 2c, 2d, 2e and 3b. Applicant contends the keys/legends in those figures are sufficient. The Examiner maintains the drawing objection in part: graphs used for quantitative or comparative presentation must include ordinate (Y-axis) labels that clearly identify the plotted quantity and units where applicable. If Applicant believes a figure’s legend provides the necessary identification, Applicant should either (a) submit replacement figure sheets that include clear Y-axis labels (and units where appropriate) for the listed figures, or (b) provide a clear written explanation pointing to specification text that unambiguously identifies the ordinate(s) and units for each contested figure and confirm that replacement figures are unnecessary. Replacement sheets must comply with 37 C.F.R. § 1.121(d) and be labeled appropriately. Until the axis-label issue is corrected or formally disclaimed, the drawing objection will remain outstanding but will not by itself prevent further examination of claim issues.
Claim Formalities and 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (Indefiniteness)
- Background: The June 13, 2016 Office action raised multiple claim informalities and 112(b) issues (IPPLGGCBRXEAPX1). Applicant amended many claims and submitted remarks disputing the 112 rejections (ITEPH30ORXEAPX4). The Examiner has reviewed the amendments and applicant remarks.
- Determination: Some informalities were corrected by Applicant’s claim amendments (for example, antecedent language in several places was clarified). Nonetheless, 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejections are maintained for the pending claims in part because the claims, even as amended, contain terms and formulations that are vague or lack clear antecedent basis or clear claim scope for examination. Representative unresolved issues are summarized below and example corrective actions are suggested.
  1) "Representative future wind speed values": The phrase remains in independent claim 1 and several dependents. The claims do not define what "representative" means in the claim context (representative of what: averages, measurements at particular rotor sections, modal values, statistical summaries?), nor do they limit the form of the representative values. The specification contains multiple possible meanings (single-value assumption, per-sector values, LIDAR upstream estimates, empirical statistical adjustments). Because the claim language covers multiple different constructions without clear limiting language, it is indefinite as written. To resolve, Applicant may (a) define the term in the claim (e.g., "wherein 'representative future wind speed values' are one or more future wind speed estimates for the rotor swept area obtained from an upstream LIDAR measurement and optionally adjusted using site-specific empirical statistics"), or (b) amend to remove the adjectival term 'representative' and use precise wording (e.g., "future wind speed estimates").
  2) Singular vs. plural and antecedent basis: Several dependent claims (e.g., original claims 6, 7 / amended claims 6, 7) use singular wording such as "the wind speed value" while the parent claims recite "values". It is unclear whether a single value or multiple values are intended. Amend to consistent pluralization or otherwise clarify.
  3) "Assuming the wind speed value to be constant over a rotor swept area": It is unclear whether this is an additional method step (i.e., a step of assuming) or a limitation of the estimating step. For clarity, recast as either an additional step (e.g., "further comprising assuming that the representative future wind speed values are constant over the rotor swept area") or a limiting clause modifying the estimating step (e.g., "wherein the estimating assumes that the representative future wind speed values are constant over the rotor swept area").
  4) Cost-function terminology and antecedent basis: Applicant amended claim 1 to recite particular cost-function choices (converted aerodynamic energy; electrical energy + kinetic energy; electrical energy while setting a rotor-speed boundary condition). Some dependent claims still reference "the electrical energy generated" or "the converted aerodynamic energy" without explicit antecedent definitions; this creates ambiguity as to whether these are distinct items or synonyms for the "energy output" recited in claim 1. To resolve, ensure each term has explicit antecedent or be stated in claim 1 as alternative embodiments (e.g., 'wherein the cost function is one of: (a) ...; (b) ...; (c) ...') and remove later dependent claims that reintroduce ambiguity.
  5) "Model Predictive Control strategy / non-linear Model Predictive Control strategy": For examination purposes, the Examiner construes these to require the control strategy utilize a predictive model (linear or non-linear). If Applicant intends these terms to carry special algorithmic meaning, Applicant should either (a) recite more specific structural or algorithmic steps (prediction horizon length, model equations, optimizer type), or (b) point to specific, unambiguous support in the specification demonstrating the exact algorithmic limitations intended.
- Conclusion on 112(b): For the reasons above, the Examiner maintains the 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejection as to the pending claims. Applicant may overcome the rejection by amendment or by explicitly identifying precise supporting passages in the specification that unambiguously define the disputed terms and by clarifying singular/plural inconsistencies. If Applicant submits an amendment that clarifies the claim scope in the suggested manner, the Examiner will reconsider the 112(b) standing.
Obviousness Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103
- Background: The June 13 Office action rejected the claims as obvious over Spruce et al. (US 2013/0106107 A1) in view of Kusiak et al. for general claims and added Hammerum (WO 2010/060772 A2) for claims reciting deformable trailing edge sections. Applicant filed arguments and amendments (ITEPH30ORXEAPX4) asserting the amended cost functions are not taught or suggested by the cited references and thus the rejections should be withdrawn.
- Examiner analysis and determination: The combined teachings of Spruce and Kusiak (and Hammerum where relevant) still provide the teachings relied upon in the original action. The Examiner finds the following points persuasive support for the 103 rejections as previously articulated:
  • Spruce discloses use of upstream wind sensing (including LIDAR) to predict wind in a future time window and a predictive controller that optimizes a cost function over a finite horizon (see original Office action citations and IPPLGGCBRXEAPX1 statements referencing Spruce: "sensor 15, including LIDAR system 26, is used to predict future wind speed values" and "predictive controller 27" optimizing a cost function). Those disclosures correspond to the claimed predictive estimation and horizon-based optimization aspects. (See IPPLGGCBRXEAPX1.)
  • Kusiak discloses optimization of energy capture / power using controllable parameters including pitch and generator torque and models that include rotor-speed dynamics; figures and discussion in Kusiak address maximizing energy captured and set up cost/objective functions related to power/energy and rotor-speed constraints. Thus Kusiak supplies teachings regarding energy-based objectives and the explicit use of torque and pitch as decision variables. (See IPPLGGCBRXEAPX1 passages quoting Kusiak: "The two controllable parameters [are] pitch angle x1 and generator torque x2"; "Maximizing energy captured from the wind").
  • Hammerum discloses deformable trailing-edge sections and control thereof, supplying the missing teaching for claims that recite deformable trailing edges.
- Taken together, Spruce's upstream prediction and predictive control and Kusiak's energy-maximizing control and torque/pitch control render the claimed subject matter obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art because the combination provides a reasoned basis to apply the energy-maximization objective with predictive wind estimates and torque/pitch control to improve energy capture. Applicant's amendment to recite particular alternative forms of the cost function does not, by itself, point to a non-obvious difference because Kusiak and Spruce address energy-related objectives and predictive control; the combination teaches using energy-based objectives over a prediction horizon with constraints relating to rotor speed and actuator penalties. For those reasons the Examiner maintains the 103 rejections for the pending claims.
- How to overcome the 103 rejections: Applicant may overcome the 103 rejections by one or more of the following:
  1) Amend the claims to add a limiting feature not suggested by Spruce+Kusiak (and Hammerum where relevant). Examples: a specific mathematical form of the cost function tied to a prediction model and constraints that produce a provable technical effect not suggested by the cited art; a particular predictor structure or horizon tied to LIDAR measurement characteristics; a novel constraint or soft-constraint implementation shown in the specification and not taught by the cited art.
  2) Submit persuasive objective evidence (e.g., experimental data, test reports, model-based comparative results) showing unexpected results achieved by the claimed combination that would not have been predicted by one of ordinary skill in view of the cited references.
  3) Argue facts of non-analogous art, lack of motivation to combine the references, or that the combined references fail to teach or suggest a specific limitation (with precise citations). Broad attorney argument alone is not persuasive; point-by-point record citations and factual showings are required.
Disposition and Requirements for Next Reply
- The Examiner maintains the 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and 103 rejections for the pending claims as set forth above. Claims cancelled by Applicant (8, 9, 11, 13) are given no further consideration.
- Applicant's reply may consist of one or any combination of the following:
  • Amend claims to address the identified 112(b) clarity issues (as discussed above) and, if appropriate, to add limitations that distinguish over the cited references.
  • Provide claim-by-claim remarks addressing the Examiner’s 112(b) findings and 103 rationale with pinpoint citations to the specification in support of claim language (for example, identify exact page/line ranges where a disputed term is defined unequivocally). If Applicant relies on specification disclosure to overcome a 112(b) objection, state the exact location(s) of support. The Examiner will only accept clear, specific citation-based support.
  • Provide persuasive evidence (test data or declarations) or argument (with record citations) that the combined prior art does not teach or suggest every claimed limitation or that the combination would not have been made by one of ordinary skill for the stated purpose.
  • If Applicant elects to file amended drawings instead of arguing axis-label sufficiency, submit replacement drawing sheets complying with 37 C.F.R. § 1.121(d) that include explicit Y-axis labels (and units where applicable) for Figures 1, 2b-2e, and 3b, or provide a written explanation with precise specification citations that unambiguously identify the plotted quantities and units for each figure.
- If Applicant files an amendment, provide a clean set of claims (with changes highlighted or an explanation of the amendments) and identify the specific support in the original/specification for any newly recited language. If Applicant files new evidence (declarations, test reports), please comply with the evidence rules (e.g., identification of declarant, attestation of authenticity, foundation, etc.).
Limitations
- The Examiner relied on the record available at the June 13, 2016 Office action and Applicant’s September 22, 2016 submissions. The Examiner's characterization of Spruce, Kusiak and Hammerum are based on the references cited in the June 13 action as summarized in that action (IPPLGGCBRXEAPX1). The Examiner's conclusions about what the references teach for prosecution purposes follow reasonable claim constructions used to permit meaningful prior art comparison; these constructions were stated in the June 13 action and applied here.
- If Applicant submits further amendments that change claim scope materially from what is presently pending, the Examiner will re-evaluate 103 in light of the new scope and may require new prior art or reframe the rejections accordingly.
- If Applicant believes any factual statement in this communication is incorrect, identify the specific statement, provide the correct citation or evidence, and the Examiner will reconsider.
Examiner's Contact
If Applicant believes telephone discussion would clarify the issues and aid in resolving outstanding matters, contact the Examiner by telephone during normal hours. A response to this action must be timely filed and must address the outstanding rejections and objections detailed above.
END OF COMMUNICATION

claim_ground_evidence.rationale: The pending independent claims as amended recite a neutral connector that makes an electrical connection with a neutral bar on the top of the neutral bar, a shield with a connector side abutting the neutral connector, and a bias spring abutting a spring side of the shield opposite the connector side. The previously applied reference Samuelson (US 2014/0321005) was relied upon in the January 13, 2017 Office action as disclosing a plug-on neutral clip assembly (including conductive clip members and an insulating cover) that performs the same structural and functional role as the claimed neutral connector, shield, and bias spring and which is shown and described in Samuelson Figures 2A/2B/3/4A/4B and accompanying description. The prior Office action identified Samuelson as disclosing a neutral connector (27) that makes electrical connection with a neutral bar (110), a shield/cover (28), and a bias spring/upper member (26) cooperating to bias the connector. Applicant's amendments rephrase the relationships among those parts but do not introduce features that are absent from the Samuelson disclosure as relied upon in the prior action; therefore the anticipation rejection is maintained for the current claim language on the present record.

evidence.support_span: Samuelson discloses a circuit breaker neutral connector (27) assembly (FIGS. 2A, 2B), comprising: a neutral connector (27) including a first side configured to make electrical connection with a neutral bar (110; FIG. 3), a shield (28) of an insulating material abutting a second side of the neutral connector (27) opposite the first side, and a bias spring (26) abutting the shield (28) and configured to bias the neutral connector (27; FIG. 4A, see also Claim 17 of Samuelson).

Regarding Claim 12, Samuelson discloses a circuit breaker, comprising: a housing (10h, including cover 28; FIGS. 4A and 4B) including a pocket (formed by the curvature of 28; FIG. 4B), and a neutral connector assembly (25) at least partially received in the pocket (FIG. 4B), the neutral connector assembly comprising: a neutral connector (27) including a first side (an end portion of 27 in contact with 110; FIGS. 3 and 4A) configured to make electrical connection with a neutral bar (110)...

claim_ground_evidence.rationale: Dependent claims recite elements (e.g., first and second prongs, extension stops, uprights alongside a shield, spring received in a recess/post, alignment feature/groove) that the prior Office action identified in Samuelson. The record shows Samuelson's connector includes prongs/uprights, top/extension stop structure, an insulating cover that aligns/receives the conductive member, and a biasing member, which correspond to the dependent claim limitations. On the present record these claims remain anticipated by the same Samuelson disclosure relied on previously.

evidence.support_span: Regarding Claim 2, Samuelson discloses ... a first prong and a second prong ... being spaced ... to receive the neutral bar therein.
Regarding Claim 3, Samuelson discloses a first extension stop ... configured to engage with a first limit stop.
Regarding Claim 7, Samuelson discloses ... first upright and a second upright ... extend alongside of the shield.
Regarding Claim 8, Samuelson discloses that the bias spring is received in a recess or on a post of the shield.
Regarding Claim 10, Samuelson discloses that the shield comprises an alignment feature configured to engage and align the neutral connector to the shield.

claim_ground_evidence.rationale: Claims 5 and 16 recite a second extension stop configured to engage with a second limit stop. The prior Office action determined Samuelson discloses an extension stop on the neutral connector but not a specifically claimed second limit stop; however, the addition of a second limit stop would have been an obvious design choice to one of ordinary skill to ensure secure positioning of a floating connector. On the present record and relying on the rationale given previously (St. Regis Paper Co. v. Bemis Co. precedent cited in the Office action), the prima facie obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 is maintained.

The prior Office action combined Samuelson with Cornell (US 3,001,172) which discloses a conductor wire fastened to a connector. On the present record that combination provides a prima facie basis under 35 U.S.C. 103 to reject claims 6 and 17 and the rejection is maintained.

applicant_argument_responses.argument_summary: Applicant amended claim 1 to recite that the neutral connector makes "an electrical connection with a neutral bar on a top of the neutral bar" and that the shield has a connector side abutting the connector and a spring side abutting the bias spring (a spring - shield - connector order). Applicant argued Samuelson discloses clamping against opposing/side walls of the neutral bar and thus does not disclose connection on the top or the claimed spring-shield-connector arrangement.
applicant_argument_responses.response: The examiner has considered the amendment and the applicant's argument. The prior Office action (January 13, 2017) relied on Samuelson's disclosure and accompanying figures (see the Office action citations to Samuelson and its Figures 2A/2B/3/4A/4B). The record cites Samuelson as disclosing a neutral connector that contacts neutral bar 110 (see the Office action statement: "a neutral connector (27) including a first side configured to make electrical connection with a neutral bar (110; FIG. 3)"). On the present record, Samuelson's conductive clip members and the associated cover/insulating member and biasing structure were found to perform the function of making electrical connection to the neutral bar and of being biased by a spring-like member abutting the insulating cover. The applicant's rephrasing to explicitly say "on a top of the neutral bar" does not identify a structural or functional feature that is absent from Samuelson as previously applied. In addition, Samuelson's Figures and description cited in the prior action were relied upon as showing the conductive member engaging the neutral bar end/face region identified in the disclosure. Therefore the rejection is maintained. If applicant believes specific portions of Samuelson (paragraphs, figure callouts) do not read on the amended limitation, applicant should (a) point to specific passages in Samuelson that do not disclose the recited limitation and explain why those passages fail to disclose it, or (b) propose further claim amendments that clearly distinguish over the identified Samuelson passages, accompanied by support in the present specification for any new narrowing language.
applicant_argument_responses.support_span: Samuelson discloses a circuit breaker neutral connector (27) assembly (FIGS. 2A, 2B), comprising: a neutral connector (27) including a first side configured to make electrical connection with a neutral bar (110; FIG. 3)...

applicant_argument_responses.argument_summary: Applicant argued Samuelson does not disclose a shield having a connector side abutting the neutral connector and a bias spring abutting a spring side of the shield opposite the connector side (i.e., a spring - shield - connector structure). Applicant asserted Samuelson instead discloses a shield - upper connector - lower connector structure.
applicant_argument_responses.response: The examiner considered the applicant's characterization. The prior Office action identified Samuelson's cover, conductive clip members, and biasing member as corresponding elements. The claims at issue recite an arrangement in which the biasing member abuts a spring side of the shield opposite the connector side; on the present record Samuelson's described and depicted assembly (as cited in the prior Office action) was found to encompass the claimed relative arrangement of insulating cover, conductive member, and biasing element. If applicant contests that Samuelson lacks the claimed relative arrangement, applicant should (i) identify the specific Samuelson passages or figures that, in applicant's view, cannot be read to disclose the claimed arrangement and provide a concise explanation, and/or (ii) further amend the claims in a manner supported by the present specification to add clarifying structural limitations that exclude Samuelson's arrangement (for example, specifying a particular geometry, relative position, or mounting detail that appears in the present specification but not in Samuelson).
applicant_argument_responses.support_span: Samuelson does not disclose or suggest a shield having a connector side abutting a neutral connector and a bias spring abutting a spring side of the shield opposite the connector side (that is, a spring - shield - connector structure).

applicant_argument_responses.argument_summary: Applicant argued Cornell does not cure deficiencies in Samuelson and does not disclose the features added in the amended independent claims.
applicant_argument_responses.response: The examiner acknowledges applicant's point that Cornell was cited only to supply the conductor wire fastened to a neutral connector element missing from Samuelson's explicit disclosure. The combination rejection for claims 6 and 17 under 35 U.S.C. 103 is premised on Samuelson as the primary reference and Cornell for the teaching of a conductor wire fastened to a connector. If applicant believes Cornell is not analogous, or the combination is improper, applicant should explain why Cornell is not combinable with Samuelson or present argumentation why the combination would not have been made by one of ordinary skill. Alternatively, applicant may amend to include additional structural limitations (supported in the present specification) that Cornell does not disclose, thereby distinguishing the claim.
applicant_argument_responses.support_span: Claims 6 and 17 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Samuelson in view of Cornell.

DETAILED ACTION
Introduction
Claims 1-20 are pending. The application remains under examination. The Office action dated January 13, 2017 (record document IXSXY3W6RXEAPX4) issued statutory rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) and 103 over Samuelson (US 2014/0321005) and, for certain dependent claims, Samuelson in view of Cornell (US 3,001,172). Applicant filed amendments to claims 1, 12, and 20 and argued against the prior rejections in the Reply dated March 28, 2017 (J0WJX2FYPXXIFW1 and J0WJX2HYPXXIFW1). The amendments and arguments have been considered. This communication is the examiner's response to the applicant's filed amendments and arguments and states the examiner's position and the reasons therefor.
Amendment Status
The Office records indicate that amendments to claims 1, 12, and 20 were presented on March 28, 2017 (document J0WJX2FYPXXIFW1). Those amendments are entered as proposed amendments with entry_status unknown in the record extract provided to the examiner. The current Office position set forth below addresses the amended claim language as presented in that submission. Applicant is advised that if the proposed claim language is desired as the official claim set, any necessary formal amendments (mark-up, redline/clean, etc.) should be filed in accordance with USPTO practice and the claims will be entered consistent with USPTO procedures.
Reexamination of Grounds in View of Applicant's Amendments and Arguments
1) 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) rejections (Samuelson)
Summary of examiner determination: The prior 102(a)(2) rejections over Samuelson for independent claims 1, 12, and 20 and many dependent claims are maintained on the present record. The January 13, 2017 Office action identified Samuelson's conductive clip assembly (including conductive member(s), insulating cover, and biasing/upper member) and corresponding figure callouts and descriptions as disclosing the same structural elements and functional relationships recited in the claims as amended. The applicant's amendments and arguments have been considered but do not supply record evidence sufficient to overcome the prior finding that Samuelson discloses the claimed elements and their arrangement.
Discussion and reasoning: The applicant amended claims 1, 12, and 20 to add express phraseology describing the neutral connector's electrical connection "with a neutral bar on a top of the neutral bar," a shield having a "connector side" abutting the neutral connector and a "spring side" abutting the bias spring opposite the connector side, and corresponding method language referencing connection "to the top of the neutral bar." The applicant argues that Samuelson discloses only clamping to opposing side walls of a neutral bar and therefore does not disclose connection on the top of the neutral bar or the claimed spring - shield - connector arrangement.
The prior Office action cited Samuelson's disclosure and figures as showing a conductive clip member (identified as element 27 in Samuelson) with an end portion in contact with neutral bar 110 and an insulating cover/shield (28) cooperating with an upper/bias member (26) and associated housing. The Office action expressly stated that Samuelson discloses a neutral connector (27) including a first side configured to make electrical connection with a neutral bar (110; FIG. 3), a shield (28) of an insulating material abutting a second side of the neutral connector opposite the first side, and a bias spring (26) abutting the shield and configured to bias the neutral connector. Those statements are in the record and form the basis for the prior rejections (see IXSXY3W6RXEAPX4).
On the present record, the examiner finds that Samuelson's conductive clip(s) and cover reflect the claimed structural relationship wherein a conductive member engages the neutral bar and the insulating cover/shield cooperates with a biasing member to bias the conductive member. The applicant's reformulation of the positional relationship (stating "top of the neutral bar" and naming connector vs. spring sides of the shield) does not, on the present record, introduce a material distinction that is not encompassed by Samuelson's disclosure as relied upon in the Office action. Samuelson's figures and descriptive text were relied on in the prior action to support the correspondence between Samuelson elements and the claimed elements. Therefore the 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) rejections over Samuelson are maintained for the amended independent claims and those dependent claims that were previously rejected under 102 in the January 13, 2017 action.
Applicant response guidance: If applicant believes that Samuelson in fact does not disclose the claimed "top of the neutral bar" contact or the claimed relative arrangement spring - shield - connector, applicant should do one of the following: (a) point to specific Samuelson passages or figure callouts and explain precisely why each recited claim limitation is absent from those passages/figures, or (b) propose further amendments adding clear, supported structural limitations from the present specification that distinguish over the specific Samuelson passages identified, and provide pointer(s) to support in the specification for any added limiting language. Broad conclusory statements that Samuelson 'only clamps sides' without citation to the particular portions of Samuelson or without claim amendments that capture a distinguishing structural detail are insufficient to overturn the present record finding.
2) 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections (Samuelson; Samuelson + Cornell)
Claims 5 and 16 (second extension stop/second limit stop): The prior action found Samuelson teaches an extension stop but not an explicitly claimed second limit stop; nevertheless, the addition of a second limit stop was found to be within routine design choice and thus obvious. That reasoning remains on the record and the 103 rejection is maintained. If applicant believes the combination of references or the rationale for obviousness is improper, applicant should present argument or submit amendments adding structural detail (supported in the present specification) that distinguishes from Samuelson's teaching.
Claims 6 and 17 (neutral conductor wire fastened to neutral connector): The prior action combined Samuelson with Cornell for the fastened conductor wire limitation. That combination and associated reasoning are maintained on the present record. If applicant disputes the combination, applicant should explain why Cornell is not combinable or propose narrowing amendments supported by the present specification.
Conclusion and Next Steps
The record as presently constituted supports maintaining the rejections: the 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) rejections of independent claims 1, 12, and 20 and the identified dependent claims over Samuelson are maintained; the 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections of claims 5 and 16 over Samuelson and of claims 6 and 17 over Samuelson in view of Cornell are maintained.
Applicant is invited to respond to this communication by one or more of the following:
- Present persuasive argument with citations to the applied references and/or to the present specification that demonstrates why the cited Samuelson passages and figures do not disclose the presently claimed limitations as interpreted; and/or
- Amend the claims to add clear, supported structural limitations that distinguish over the specific Samuelson disclosures relied upon in the prior action; or
- If applicant believes a claim set is now allowable, provide a clean set of claims in the formal amendment format for entry and consideration.
If applicant provides further amendments, the examiner will consider them and any accompanying arguments and will take appropriate further action (which may include withdrawal of a rejection if the amendment overcomes the cited references, or issuance of a subsequent Office action if the rejections are maintained or other issues are found). The present communication is non-final; applicant may continue prosecution in the normal course by filing a response within the statutory period.
References relied upon in the prior action (for convenience in preparing applicant's response): Samuelson (US 2014/0321005) as cited in IXSXY3W6RXEAPX4; Cornell (US 3,001,172) as cited in IXSXY3W6RXEAPX4.
No allowance is entered at this time. Further prosecution is invited per the guidance above.

parsed.office_action:
Examiner Action — Non-Final Rejection (Mailing date: [date of action])

A. Claims Under Consideration and Procedural Background
Claims 1–4, 6–10, 14, 16 and 18–21 are currently pending. Applicant elected the species corresponding to the Figure 2 embodiment (the elected species) during the restriction requirement and identified claims 1–4 and 6–21 for continued prosecution on the elected species. The record includes the Office restriction/rejection mailed October 4, 2016 (ITPYMYW7RXEAPX4) which sets forth prior-art rejections over Hayashi and combinations with Jin and Zang. Applicant filed an amendment and arguments dated February 6, 2017 (IYUQ7HZ3RXEAPX5, IYUQ7HZ5RXEAPX5, IYUQ7HZ6RXEAPX5). The present Office action responds to the arguments and amended claim set.

B. Summary of the Examiner’s Determinations
1) The 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1) rejections of claims 1, 7–10 and 20 over Hayashi (as presented in the Office action of record) are maintained. The record supports that Hayashi discloses the structural elements recited by those claims (substrates, electrodes, PDLC and GHLC layers, and the modes of operation in which the layers transmit in one state and scatter/absorb in another). The Examiner’s prior factual finding that Hayashi provides the cited structural elements has not been rebutted by documentary evidence in the present reply.
2) The 35 U.S.C. § 103(a) rejections of claims 14–16 and 21 over Hayashi in view of Jin are maintained. Hayashi provides the multilayer liquid crystal/PDLC+GHLC teaching; Jin provides teachings about transparent display panels with transmissive/emissive areas and top-emission arrangements. The combination supplies the structural/panel-level features recited in those claims.
3) The 35 U.S.C. § 103(a) rejections of claims 2–4, 6 and 17–19 over Hayashi in view of Zang (and, where applied, further in view of Jin) are maintained. Zang teaches partitioning of liquid composition with walls and adhesive structures which the Examiner reasonably relied upon to show it would have been obvious to apply Zang’s wall/adhesive partitioning to Hayashi’s multilayer GHLC/PDLC structure to achieve sealed liquid crystal areas and desired mechanical adhesion between alignment films.

C. Response to Applicant Arguments (A1)
Applicant’s primary argument (IYUQ7HZ6RXEAPX5 REM and IYUQ7HZ3RXEAPX5 A1) asserts that Zang does not teach a wall with a concavo-convex shape and does not disclose adhered first and second alignment films that encompass GHLC material; applicant further argues Hayashi and Jin do not supply those specific structures.

Examiner Response:
- The Examiner acknowledges applicant’s point of emphasis regarding the particular wording "concavo-convex" and the particular arrangement of adhered alignment films. However, for both anticipation and obviousness inquiries the key question is whether the claimed structural elements are taught or would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art in view of the cited art. The October 4, 2016 Office action put applicant on notice that Hayashi supplies the multilayer PDLC/GHLC teachings and that Zang supplies wall/adhesive partitioning teachings (ITPYMYW7RXEAPX4). The Examiner relied on Zang's teaching of walls and adhesive on or near the wall to supply the claimed partitioning and sealing structure in combination with Hayashi's multilayer arrangement.
- Applicant’s reply is argumentative but does not present new documentary evidence—e.g., a copy of Zang with highlighted passages showing an absence of relevant structures nor a declaration or other evidence establishing that one skilled in the art would not combine Zang’s partitioning with Hayashi’s multilayer structure. Absent such evidence, the Examiner maintains the rejections because the cited references disclose the structural elements or provide a clear rationale for combination. The Examiner also notes that functional language in applicant’s claims (modes realized upon application or removal of voltage) is given patentable weight only to the extent it corresponds to structural elements. The PDLC and GHLC structural elements in Hayashi are what enable the claimed modes; therefore the Examiner continues to rely on Hayashi for those mode-related limitations.

D. Specific Points Where Applicant May Amend or Submit Evidence
1) If applicant contends the claims require a specific geometry (for example, a particular concavo-convex wall profile or a specific manner of adhesion of two alignment films) that neither Hayashi nor Zang discloses, applicant may amend the claims to add explicit structural limitations (for example, a recitation of wall geometry parameters, materials or a structural fastening/adhesive layer with defined placement). Adding such structural limitations may avoid the present combinations.
2) If applicant has documentary evidence that Zang lacks the wall/adhesive teaching relied upon by the Examiner, applicant should submit a clearly marked copy of Zang pointing to the passages supporting that position, or a declaration explaining why a skilled artisan would not have combined the cited references or why such combination would have been unpredictable.
3) Applicant may also file proposed substitute claims that further limit the elected species to structural features not present in the cited art.

E. Conclusion and Next Steps
For the reasons given above and supported by the record (see citations in Section B), the rejections under 35 U.S.C. §§ 102 and 103 identified in the October 4, 2016 Office action are maintained with respect to the currently pending claims listed at the top of this action. Applicant’s traverse has been considered but is not persuasive of patentability in view of the currently cited prior art and the present claim scope.

Applicant is invited to reply by:
- Amending the claims to include additional structural limitations that distinguish over the applied references; and/or
- Presenting documentary evidence or a declaration that directly rebuts the Examiner’s basis for combination (for example, a copy of Zang with highlighted passages and explanation); and/or
- Presenting persuasive argument explaining why a skilled artisan would not have combined the specific teachings of Hayashi and Zang/Jin to arrive at the claimed subject matter.

If applicant files amended claims, include a claim listing showing changes, and indicate any dependent claims that remain. If applicant files evidence, it should be submitted as an information disclosure or with an appropriate affidavit/declaration as required.

F. Administrative Notes
- The examiner confirms applicant’s election of the Figure 2 species and acknowledges the amendment to the title (IYUQ7HZ4RXEAPX5). The title objection is considered addressed by the amendment.
- If applicant requests an interview to discuss the references and potential claim amendments, the examiner is available; contact information is on the record.

(571) 270-1428

(End of Office Action)

Examination Summary
This communication responds to the Applicant’s Amendment and Remarks filed November 11, 2014 (Paper Nos. I2DJ7BAAPXXIFW3, I2HILX7EPXXIFW1, I2HILX8NPXXIFW1). The prior Office action of record (July 15, 2014; HXHKWXTQPXXIFW4) rejected the pending claims under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) and, in the alternative, under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) over Yagishita (US 2005/0107269) and, as a secondary reference for the 103 rejections, McConnachie (US 2001/0053751). Applicant has amended claims and argued against the rejections. After consideration of the amendments and arguments, the rejections are continued for the reasons given below.
Claims and Status
- Claims 1–4 as entered earlier remain of record (HOHGC4B3PXXIFW2). Applicant’s November 11, 2014 submission proposes amended Claim 1 and adds Claims 5–6 (I2HILX7EPXXIFW1). The Examiner treats the newly presented claim set as pending for examination and addresses the amendments and arguments.
Summary of Grounds
1) 35 U.S.C. 102(b) — anticipation by Yagishita: maintained.
2) 35 U.S.C. 103(a) — obviousness over Yagishita in view of McConnachie: maintained.
Substantive Reasons for Maintenance of Rejections
1. Anticipation (35 U.S.C. 102)
- The Examiner’s earlier Office action explained the factual basis for the 102(b) rejection: Yagishita discloses a lubricating oil composition containing a phosphorus compound corresponding to the claimed formula (1), a sulfur-containing molybdenum compound, and an ashless dispersant; Yagishita includes example formulations with molybdenum-containing additives having Mo and S contents in the numerical region claimed. See the July 15, 2014 Office action (HXHKWXTQPXXIFW4) where the Examiner stated: "Claims 1-4 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as being anticipated by, or in the alternative rendered obvious by Yagishita." The application publication in the record (applicant’s own published specification and examples) explicitly identifies a molybdenum dithiocarbamate with numerical Mo and S contents and a stated Mo:S of "1:3.81" in the example footnote (*7) (pgpub_description). That disclosure shows a molybdenum dithiocarbamate species with a Mo:S relation at the numerical threshold that Applicant now attempts to recite in amended claim 1 (1:3.81) and in claim 6 (1:4 or greater). Because the record includes a disclosed molybdenum dithiocarbamate having Mo:S = 1:3.81, the amendment to require 1:3.81 does not avoid the ground that the claimed subject matter is disclosed by the prior-art composition(s) (as applied in the July 15, 2014 Office action). The 102(b) rejection is therefore maintained.
- Note regarding a record inconsistency: the Examiner’s July 15, 2014 Office action described Yagishita’s compound 6 in Table 4 as having certain Mo and S values (HXHKWXTQPXXIFW4). The applicant’s published application (pgpub_description) includes a Table 1 with footnote *7 explicitly stating "Mo content: 9.0 mass %, sulfur content: 12.0 mass %, Mo:S = 1:3.81." Both documents are in the record; the presence of an identified molybdenum dithiocarbamate with Mo:S = 1:3.81 in the record supports continuing the rejection of claims that adopt that numerical threshold. If Applicant believes there is a specific, substantive discrepancy in the cited prior art that affects patentability, Applicant should identify the exact passage in the cited prior art and explain why that passage does not disclose the claimed limitation, or submit evidence demonstrating the absence of such a disclosure.
2. Obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103)
- The 103 rejection over Yagishita in view of McConnachie is continued. The Examiner’s combination rationale is that Yagishita furnishes the lubricating composition framework (phosphorus compound per formula (1), molybdenum sulfur-containing species, ashless dispersants) and that McConnachie discloses oil-soluble molybdenum–sulfur species (trinuclear Mo–S compounds) known in the lubrication art. Replacing or selecting a particular Mo–S species known in the art to achieve expected friction/wear benefits is within the routine skill of the ordinarily skilled artisan. The Examiner’s July 15, 2014 action explained that McConnachie teaches oil-soluble trinuclear Mo–S compounds and that substituting known Mo–S compounds into the composition of Yagishita to achieve predictable effects is an obvious design choice. See HXHKWXTQPXXIFW4: "McConnachie discloses an oil-soluble tri-nuclear molybdenum-sulfur compound... It would have been obvious... to use the compounds of McConnachie in the composition of Yagishita... to obtain predictable results." This reasoning applies to the currently pending claims and to the newly added claims because the record shows Mo–S species within or near the numerical limits recited.
Applicant Arguments and Examiner Responses
- Applicant argues that Yagishita does not teach or suggest a Mo:S ratio of 1:3.81 or 1:4, and that McConnachie’s trinuclear Mo–S compounds are different from the claimed (B1)/(B2) species (Remarks, I2HILX8NPXXIFW1). The Examiner has considered these arguments. The record contains a disclosure (applicant’s own publication) of a molybdenum dithiocarbamate with "Mo content: 9.0 mass %, sulfur content: 12.0 mass %, Mo:S = 1:3.81" (pgpub_description, Table 1 footnote *7). That disclosure demonstrates that a Mo–S ratio at applicant’s amended threshold appears in the record. Therefore, the amendment to require 1:3.81 does not establish a novel numerical limitation over the cited disclosure in the Office action. Regarding McConnachie, the Examiner’s use of that reference is as a secondary reference to show other known Mo–S species that a practitioner could select; applicant’s characterization that the McConnachie cores are different does not, without persuasive technical evidence or factual showing of non-analogousness or teaching away, rebut the Examiner’s prima facie case of obviousness.
Action Required / Options to Applicant
- The present non‑final rejection is maintained. Applicant may respond by one or more of the following: (a) file amendments to the claims that explicitly and clearly distinguish over the cited passages of Yagishita (and McConnachie) — for example, by adding limitations not disclosed or suggested by the cited art; (b) submit persuasive evidence showing that the cited prior art does not disclose or render obvious the claimed subject matter (for example, a declaration under 37 C.F.R. § 1.132 showing factual differences, or comparative data showing unexpected results attributable to the claimed features); or (c) argue why the combination rationale is improper by pointing to specific teachings in the cited references that teach away from the proposed combinations or by explaining why the particular Mo–S species and numerical thresholds are not analogous, routine or predictable selections.
- If Applicant believes the Examiner has mischaracterized a specific passage in the cited references (for example, disputing the numerical Mo and S values attributed to an example), identify the exact passage(s) in the cited reference(s) and provide a clear explanation and, if available, documentary support.
Conclusion
Because the record contains explicit disclosure of molybdenum sulfur-containing species at or near the numerical thresholds claimed and because the Examiner’s combination rationale for obviousness remains supported by the cited references, the prior 102(b) and 103(a) rejections are maintained. This is a non-final action. Applicant’s timely response should (i) propose claim language that distinguishes over the cited material, or (ii) present persuasive argument or evidence to overcome the rejections. The Examiner is willing to consider amendments and evidence and will re-evaluate the grounds in light of any such timely submission.
